summary: Sirach 12 counsels readers to be careful about whom they help and trust. The chapter moves from selective generosity toward the godly and lowly, to warnings that friendship and enmity are revealed in changing circumstances, to vivid cautions about an enemy who may use closeness, soft speech, or apparent help to harm.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach applying wisdom to social risk: alms, friendship, enemies, and judgment under pressure. It also raises one of the book’s harder tensions, because its call to give wisely is stated alongside severe warnings about sinners and enemies.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the book into Greek.
context.audience: Originally students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem; later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: Hebrew composition in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; Greek translation after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: compact poetic teaching and practical maxims for conduct in ordinary social life.

outline.heading: Discern Whom You Help
outline.note: Good deeds and alms are urged, but the reader is told to know the recipient and not expect good from one who continues in evil.

outline.heading: Give to the Godly, Not the Sinner
outline.note: The instruction repeats a contrast between helping the godly or good person and not strengthening the sinner or ungodly person.

outline.heading: Prosperity and Adversity Reveal People
outline.note: Friend and enemy are tested differently when a person prospers or suffers.

outline.heading: Do Not Trust an Enemy’s Humility
outline.note: The enemy’s wickedness is compared to corrosion, and the reader is warned not to place such a person close enough to take one’s position.

outline.heading: Risky Association Brings Consequences
outline.note: The chapter compares going near a sinner to approaching snakes or wild beasts, then says such a companion will not stay when the reader falters.

outline.heading: The Enemy’s Hidden Intentions
outline.note: The enemy may speak, weep, or appear to help, but the chapter portrays him as waiting for an opportunity to harm.

keyVerses.text: If you do good, know to whom you do it, and your good deeds will have thanks.
keyVerses.why: This opening sentence states the chapter’s main concern: generosity is commended, but it is joined to discernment.

keyVerses.text: A man’s friend won’t be fully tried in prosperity. His enemy won’t be hidden in adversity.
keyVerses.why: This verse turns the chapter from giving to testing relationships through prosperity and adversity.

keyVerses.text: Never trust your enemy, for his wickedness is like corrosion in copper.
keyVerses.why: The command and image anchor the chapter’s long warning about enemies who may seem harmless.

keyVerses.text: The enemy will speak sweetly with his lips, and in his heart plan to throw you into a pit. The enemy may weep with his eyes, but if he finds opportunity, he will want more blood.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s concern about deceptive speech, hidden intent, and danger when opportunity appears.

questions.question: Is the chapter against doing good?
questions.answer: No. It begins, “If you do good,” and says good deeds can have thanks. Its concern is not whether to do good at all, but whether the giver understands the person and situation involved.

questions.question: What does “alms” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “alms” refers to giving help or charitable support. Verse 3 treats refusing alms as part of a negative pattern, while verses 4-7 warn the reader not to use giving in a way that strengthens a harmful person.

questions.question: Why does Sirach say, “don’t help the sinner”?
questions.answer: The chapter frames this as a warning about giving support that may empower someone to harm the giver or others. Readers differ over how broadly to apply this kind of wisdom saying: some read it as counsel about dangerous alliances, while others see a sharp tension with wider calls to mercy. The chapter itself gives the reason in verse 5: the recipient may “subdue you with it.”

questions.question: Does “godly man” mean the person is morally perfect?
questions.answer: The chapter does not define the phrase in detail. It contrasts the “godly man” and “good man” with the “sinner” and “ungodly,” so the basic distinction is between people aligned with good conduct and people characterized here by harmful evil.

questions.question: What is the point of prosperity and adversity in verses 8-9?
questions.answer: The chapter says circumstances reveal relationships. Prosperity can hide a friend’s true quality, while adversity can expose an enemy or reveal that even a friend leaves.

questions.question: Why compare wickedness to “corrosion in copper”?
questions.answer: The comparison presents wickedness as something that works into a material and damages it. The point is not a technical claim about metalwork, but an image of hidden, persistent deterioration that makes the enemy unsafe to trust.

questions.question: Why does the chapter warn against putting an enemy next to you or at your right hand?
questions.answer: Those images describe closeness, access, and honor. Verse 12 says the danger is that the enemy may overthrow the reader, stand in the reader’s place, or seek to take the reader’s seat.

questions.question: Are verses 13-14 blaming victims for being harmed?
questions.answer: The verses use sharp comparisons: a charmer bitten by a snake, someone approaching wild beasts, and someone associating with a sinner. The point is a warning about avoidable risk, not a full account of every case where someone suffers harm. Responsible readers should not turn this into permission to withhold compassion from victims.

questions.question: How does the chapter describe deceptive enemies?
questions.answer: It says the enemy may humble himself, speak sweetly, weep, and pretend to help. Yet the chapter also says he may plan to throw the reader into a pit, want more blood, trip the reader, whisper, and change his countenance.

glossary.def: Charitable giving or material help; in this chapter it appears in a warning about people who give no alms.
A condition of doing well or having success; the chapter says it can affect how friends and enemies appear.
Trouble or hardship; the chapter says it reveals enemies and may cause even a friend to leave.
A damaging decay or eating away; the chapter uses it as an image for an enemy’s wickedness.
A person’s face or outward expression; the chapter says the enemy will “change his countenance.”
